# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later and sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Expanse - Unlock wasted GPU capacity", 2026-05-04 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QCF-expanse-unlock-wasted-gpu-capacity
- [HN] Launch HN: "Launch HN: Expanse (YC P26) – Unlock Wasted GPU Capacity", 2026-06-01, the founders' post and the thread (27 comments), read whole through the HN Algolia API — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48356312 (https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/48356312)
- [WB] expanse.sh as archived 2026-06-01, the day of the Launch HN — https://web.archive.org/web/20260601142950/https://expanse.sh/
- [YCP] YC company page, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/expanse
- [SITE] expanse.sh, read 2026-10-22 — https://expanse.sh

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

## Respondents → the public account each is based on

Researchers (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Priyanka Raghunathan → [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work"; the fine-tuning run is the author's.
- Tobias Brandt → [HN] the genomics comment (bursty pipeline, "about 8 different steps", "We need to reserve the $MAX requirements for each").
- Ana Lucía Ferreira → [HN] the student's "so I overestimate" on simulation time; the queue wait for a big request is the author's.
- Kwabena Owusu → author's invention, filling a gap: an ML engineer whose sizes come from past runs on a dashboard, so the problem is not a chorus (against on Importance and Current solution).
- Mei-Ling Zhou → author's invention: a chipped (rather_not_say) story at a quant fund, GUESSED by code.
- Rafael Moreno → author's invention: a vague, habitual story (GUESSED), echoing [HN] "everyone over-requests by two to three times".
- Ingrid Haugen → author's invention: a gate No (writing up, no jobs that week).
- Samuel Adeyemi → author's invention: a gate No (away at a conference).
- Yusuf Demir → [HN] "snooping on sumbit scripts ... many of them are egregiously bad": a copied script holding eight GPUs.
- Claire Dubois-Martin → author's invention, filling a gap: a licensed binary with no source code, so the tested condition fails ('no').
- Hiroshi Takeda → [HN] "at least for everyone else, I'd would prefer tuning my own usage myself": he profiles a test run (Current solution mostly works; Adoption friction no).
- Fatima Al-Sayed → [HN] "you lose days of work"; the walltime limit and the group allocation are the author's.
- Diego Castañeda → [HN] the student's PDE simulation ("If I'm running a PDE simulation, and I allocate n machines I want to use all of them"); he keeps his margin (Adoption friction probably not).

Cluster operators (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).
- Beatrix Okoro → [HN] "What you are really left with is the 'small and medium business' clusters that are purpose specific": a small cluster, less waste, a lower rung.
- Thomas Reinholt → [HN] the security objection ("a hard no"); would not pay.
- Leilani Kahale → [HN] "In many places the cost of the HPC hardware isn't passed onto them": a grant-funded university cluster that does not measure the waste (dont_know) and has no line for a monthly fee.

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip, and 'Leave this out of the study' fits a typed-answer screen because I may not want to test this belief.
screens.why5: The belief line keeps 'the job runs first time, no resubmits' but silently drops the shorter queue wait I typed and adds 'for most' and 'their last job submission', so it does not yet say all I meant.

screens.why1: Right after I said what it does better than today's way, Keel shows me the benefit rows strangers will tick from and the belief it will test, so it is obvious why this screen is here.
screens.why2: "Resubmits" and "the queue" are everyday words on a SLURM cluster, and the intro's instruction to reword, remove or add under 9 words each is clear on first read.
screens.why3: I know what a failed run and a long queue wait cost my researchers, so I can judge both rows and the belief from what I see in their job submissions.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and in researchers' words, but the list misses the benefit I lead with, less reserved compute going unused, and the "last job submission" belief assumes a run-first-time gain even where the last job would have run anyway.
screens.why5: "Debug failures in seconds, not days" is narrowed to the job running first time, but that is the fewer-attempts advantage I gave, and the shorter queue wait is my answer too, so the meaning is kept.
screens.instead: What it does better than today's way (tick any): The job runs first time, no resubmits / A shorter wait in the queue / You stop holding GPUs the job never uses

screens.why1: After how it fits and what it does better, asking what they must do to start using it is the obvious last solution question, and the frame says 4 of 4.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain, and I can answer at once in my own words about suggested sizes and padding.
screens.why3: I built the product and watched how researchers pad their requests, so I know what it asks of them, though 'setup' sits largely with the operator who installs the agent, not the researcher.
screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip, and 'Leave this out of the study' fits a founder who decides this condition is not worth testing.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my first clause almost word for word but silently drops 'apply the line-level code fixes', and 'Most would' is Keel's addition, though the tested choice is the one I would make.

screens.why1: Right after I said what they will have to do to start using it, Keel showing its list back for me to check and pick the one to test is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Padding, suggested sizes and line-level fixes are how I and my users talk, and the repeated title in the intro costs no understanding.
screens.why3: I know from the thread and our deployments what a researcher must change, and that some keep their margin or tune their own usage, so I can judge this list from what I know.
screens.why4: The first two rows are real and distinct, but 'Submit a first job through it' is odd because jobs still go through SLURM or Kubernetes as before, with nothing new to submit through.
screens.why5: The suggested-sizes row and the belief keep my words, but 'through it' drifts from my claim that we plug into the job life cycle 'so you don't have to change how you submit things'.
screens.instead: Keep 'Use the suggested sizes instead of padding' and 'Apply the line-level code fixes it suggests', and replace the third row with 'Let it read your job scripts and code'.

screens.why1: Straight after I listed what researchers must do to start, it makes sense to ask which of those efforts is most likely to stop them, because strangers only get one question.
screens.why2: "Padding", "suggested sizes" and "line-level code fixes" are the words my trade and I already use, and the title and intro are clear on first reading.
screens.why3: As the founder, I know that researchers over-request because they fear a mid-run kill, so I can judge from what I know that trusting the sizes is the likeliest thing to stop them.
screens.why4: The first two options are real and distinct and the true answer is there, but "Submit a first job through it" is odd because Expanse hooks into SLURM or K8s so that nobody changes how they submit.
screens.why5: My belief comes back intact as "Most would use the suggested sizes instead of padding", with the picked option's wording unchanged and the test tied to that option.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop them? Use the suggested sizes instead of padding / Apply the line-level code fixes it suggests / Let it read your job scripts and source code

screens.why1: With the idea written and the beliefs picked, and just before the study goes out, it's obvious why Keel asks whether to end it by inviting people to try the product.
screens.why2: The question is short and the hint explains it, but to me a pilot is a paid deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, so I need a second read to see that here it just means collecting emails from people willing to try it.
screens.why3: I can decide whether I want those emails, but I have to guess what a yes is worth, because a researcher can't put an agent on every node and the two-week measurement is the operator's call.
screens.why4: Yes and no are complete and distinct and cover the only two choices on this screen, and no escape chip is needed.
screens.why5: My Yes is kept, but the word has drifted: my pilot is a paid one that follows a free two-week measurement and is sold to the operator, while this one is an email line, and the screen doesn't say who gets asked.
screens.instead: Ask for emails at the end? "Would you try this for real? Leave your email." You see who said yes on the Pilot tab. (Yes, ask them / No, don't ask)

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out, it is obvious why I would pick who asks my researchers the questions.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint packs video, typing, voice recording, credits and text-message delivery into one block, and 'records the voice you pick once' takes a second read.
screens.why3: I can play the two 5-second samples and decide which one I would want asking researchers about their jobs, with no outside knowledge needed.
screens.why4: The two interviewers are distinct and each has a sample to hear, and a default with a free switch needs no escape chip.
screens.why5: 'Researchers' is my word for the people I am testing with, and nothing here changes what I typed about Expanse.
screens.instead: Who should ask researchers your questions? Daphne or Saskia (tap to hear each). Researchers get a text link and can talk, type or tap; recording the voice costs 400 credits, whichever you choose.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, it is obvious that I now choose how my researchers will answer before the study goes out.
screens.why2: The choice itself is clear, but 'Daphne Daphne' and the run-together 'Hear her Still recording · ready in a few minutes' need a second read, and 'catches every spoken answer' is vaguer than I would like.
screens.why3: I know how my researchers work, often at a desk in a shared lab or office and comfortable typing, so I can decide this from what I know.
screens.why4: AI interviewer, read and tap, and letting them choose are complete and distinct, and each says when it will be ready, which is what I need to decide.
screens.why5: My pick of 'Read and tap' is kept as chosen and the screen calls my respondents researchers, as I typed them.

screens.why1: Right after choosing how researchers answer, deciding who receives a link is the obvious last step before the interviews go out.
screens.why2: The question and all three options are short and clear to me on first reading, though the Contacts page is named without having been shown in this flow.
screens.why3: I know whether I can name researchers from our cluster conversations or need to post in a place where they gather, so I can answer this from what I actually do.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel search list and one open link for a group are distinct, complete routes and cover how I would reach researchers on shared clusters.
screens.why5: My pick of people I know by name is kept exactly, and the screen changes nothing about the researchers or the idea I typed.

screens.why_b1: The verdict "Too few to call" is stated under the title with "4 answered" beside it, and each card adds "5 needed to call it", so I know nothing is decided and which number decides that.
screens.why_b2: The stage page has no chart and the bar of 5 is plain on each card, but "3 too few · 7 people answered" takes a second look: it could mean three people rather than three cards, and nothing says why 7 answered but only 4 count.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, Relative advantage and Adoption friction carry the names and belief lines I checked, word for word, even though Keel's garbled statement above them has "the researcher installed on every node".
screens.why_b4: "4 answered · 5 needed" implies I am one countable answer short on each belief, but the screen never says what that means for the idea or that I should get more answers, or from whom.
screens.why_b5: It calls nothing held or failed on 4 answers, says plainly that the number is too low, and keeps both the 4 and the 7 visible, so it makes no claim beyond the people who answered.
screens.instead: Not decided yet: 7 researchers answered, but only 4 could be counted on each belief and Keel needs 5, so get at least one more countable answer before changing the solution, and tell me why the other 3 weren't counted.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits beside the deciding number, 4 counted against 5 needed, though the headline's "4 answered" is loose because five people answered and four were counted.
screens.why_b2: What is counted and over how many people are plain (3 yes, 1 with some steps, 0 no, 4 counted), but "3 of 4 (no more than 1 in 3 say no)" sets a count of yeses beside a limit on noes, and the marker at 3 next to a ghost cell took me a second look.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and "the source code sat on the cluster" are the name and belief I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" tells me not to act on this, but not that I need one more countable answer from someone describing their real last job, or what a yes or no would mean for the idea.
screens.why_b5: It keeps the n visible, names Rafael's guess as not counted, and calls four people "a lean, not a call", so no claim goes beyond the people who answered.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 5 answered but only 4 counted, because Rafael's was a guess; all 4 lean your way with none against, so get one more researcher's real last job before relying on source code being on the cluster.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right beside the deciding number, and the So line says it plainly as 4 counted, 5 needed, though the header's "4 answered" made me look twice when five names are listed.
screens.why_b2: What is counted and over how many are plain (3 better, 1 same, of 4), but "your bar · 3 of 4" reads as if my bar were 3 of 4 when the bar is no more than 1 in 3 against, so it takes a second look.
screens.why_b3: The name and the belief line are the ones I checked, word for word, and "the job runs first time, no resubmits" is my own claim.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is true but stops there: it doesn't tell me that one more counted answer would settle this, or what Kwabena's point about sizes that are already fine means for who I should target.
screens.why_b5: The low n stays visible, the card says "a lean, not a call" and that nothing is settled, it flags the answers as a hypothetical, and it names Rafael's guess as not counted, so it claims nothing beyond the people who answered.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 5 answered but only 4 counted, and you need 5. So far 3 say a lot better and 1 says no difference, which is within your limit of 1 in 3 against, so get one more researcher's clear answer before you rely on this, and note that the one against already sizes jobs from past runs.

screens.why_b1: The verdict, Too few to call, sits right beside the number that decides it, 5 needed against 4, and the So line repeats that tie.
screens.why_b2: Four for and none against reads at once, but the base takes a second look because the top says 4 answered and the count line says 5 answered, 4 counted, while the bar is given both as 3 of 4 and as no more than 1 in 3 against, separately from the 5 needed to call it.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would use the suggested sizes instead of padding' are the name and line I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' stops the wrong conclusion and implies I am one counted answer short, but it never tells me to get one more or what to do about the two conditional yeses.
screens.why_b5: No claim goes beyond these people: the low n is stated twice, Rafael's guess is left out with the reason given, the conditional yeses are split out, and it says a lean, not a call.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 5 answered, 4 counted (Rafael's was a guess), 5 needed. All 4 lean your way, but 2 only if it is clearly worth it, so get one more counted answer and show researchers it is worth it before relying on this.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits directly beside its deciding number, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', so I know the state of the line and why it stands there.
screens.why_b3: The name Relative advantage and the belief line about the job running first time with no resubmits are exactly the ones I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The screen never says what this means for the idea or what to do next; it does not even say to get one more answer or to look at the data-and-libraries complaint.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond its people: 4 answered, 1 against, 1 asked, one quote, and the line is plainly not called.
screens.why_b6: I did not type this: an ML engineer whose sizes from past runs are already fine and whose day goes on getting data onto nodes and libraries to agree, which points at a pain beside the one I am selling against.
screens.instead: Keep the quote, and add under it: one person is too few to call, but they say sizing is already fine and their lost time is data and libraries, so get at least one more answer and ask the next researchers whether sizing or setup costs them more.

screens.why1: As the opening screen of a study about cluster jobs, it is obvious they would first check whether I actually work on a cluster of that size.
screens.why2: Run jobs, cluster and GPUs are the words I use every day, so I can answer on first reading or hearing.
screens.why3: I know roughly how many GPUs our shared cluster has and that I submit jobs to it, so I can answer from what I do.
screens.why4: Yes and No are complete and distinct for a plain fact about my cluster, and a screener carries no escape chip so none is missing.
screens.why5: It names no product or company and shows nothing of the founder's plans, only the cluster-size condition in words I would use myself.
screens.why6: It is one short question with two options that I can hold after hearing it once, and 100 and GPUs both say cleanly.

screens.why1: After asking whether I run jobs on a cluster this size, it makes sense to ask whether I recently had to resubmit one, because that picks out people who have just dealt with this problem.
screens.why2: Resubmit and resource requests are everyday words for anyone on SLURM or Kubernetes, so I can answer on first reading, though I might pause over whether a changed time limit counts.
screens.why3: I know whether I resubmitted a job with a different memory, GPU or time request this past week, because I'd have done it myself.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover the question, but the chips are off: there are two escapes where a yes-or-no gate needs none, and 'I can't recall one particular job submission' doesn't quite fit a question about whether something happened at all.
screens.why5: It asks about something I actually do in my trade's own words, and nothing about a product, a founder or their terms reaches me.
screens.why6: Said aloud, it is one short question of 14 words ending in 'Yes or no', which I can hear once and answer straight away.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did you resubmit a job with changed resource requests? Yes / No (no escape chips).

screens.why1: After being asked whether I resubmitted a job with changed resource requests, and with the kicker saying an idea to consider, a card about predicting resources at submit makes obvious sense.
screens.why2: SLURM, walltime, GPU memory and submission script are my daily words, but "predicted resources for each job" is a clipped label and "runs on every node of your own network" made me reread, since I think in terms of a cluster, not a network.
screens.why3: Guessing memory, GPUs and walltime at submit is exactly what I do, so I can weigh this against my own jobs and the time I lost to under-requesting.
screens.why4: The screen is a card to read and shows no options, rows, chips or value box.
screens.why5: It is an idea card shown on purpose so naming the product is fine, but "line-level optimisations" and "every node of your own network" read like the founder's pitch rather than words I would use.
screens.why6: It says as short sentences with no slash or parenthesis, but the fragment "At submit it reads source code, submission script and hardware" and the long list of predicts, flags and suggests is a lot to hold on one hearing, and the belief repeats the four resources rather than pointing back to the how as the guidelines ask.
screens.instead: Imagine Expanse, a tool that predicts what each job needs before you submit. It runs on your own cluster, hooked into SLURM or Kubernetes, reads your code, submission script and hardware, and tells you the GPU memory, memory, CPUs and walltime to request; if a job fails, it says why and how to fix it. The people building it believe this would give you the right request the first time.

screens.why1: It follows the idea card as a check on whether predictions could work for me, but nothing links predicted resources to where my code lives, so the jump to source code is abrupt.
screens.why2: Source code on the cluster is plain to me as someone who submits jobs, and I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I know exactly where the code for my last submitted job was, whether on the shared filesystem, in a container image or pulled from a repo.
screens.why4: Yes and No fit, but 'Yes, with some steps' is odd for a plain fact about where my code was and misses the real middle case of only part of it being there, and 'I can't tell' barely fits something I would know.
screens.why5: The idea card is shown on purpose, and the question uses ordinary trade words with no founder product terms or role labels leaking through.
screens.why6: It is short when said aloud, with one anchor, one question, three short options I can hold and one escape said last.
screens.instead: Think of your last job submission. Was its source code on the cluster when you submitted it? Yes, all of it; Only part of it; No; or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and a question about my setup, asking whether this would have helped my last submission is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: It is one short question I understand on first read, and 'job submission' is exactly how I talk about my work.
screens.why3: I know how my last job went and what I requested, but the card only says 'predicted resources', so whether it would have helped depends on how good the prediction is and I would partly be guessing.
screens.why4: The four options run cleanly from a lot better to worse without overlap, and 'I can't tell' fits since I haven't seen the predictions.
screens.why5: The only product language is the idea card shown on purpose and its name, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms for people reaches me.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, with four short options I can hold and one escape said last, so I would hear it once and answer.

screens.why1: After being asked whether Expanse would have helped, it makes sense to ask whether I would actually give up my padding to use it.
screens.why2: Padding a request is exactly what I call it on the cluster, and suggested sizes is clear enough for memory, GPUs and run time given the card above it.
screens.why3: I know how I pad and why, but without having seen a suggested size or how it fails, my answer is partly a guess, since one killed job after days of work would change it.
screens.why4: The set covers the range and the escape fits, but only the second option carries a condition, and it overlaps with Yes and Probably not because I would really mean yes if it did not kill my jobs, not simply if it was worth it.
screens.why5: The idea is shown on purpose on the card, and nothing beyond it reaches me except a plain description of what using it would ask of me.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is two short sentences forming one question, followed by four short options I can hold and one escape, with nothing that only the eye can read.
screens.instead: To use Expanse, you'd use its suggested sizes instead of padding your request. Would you do that, or not? Yes; yes, if I'd seen them hold up on my jobs first; probably not; or no. Or say you can't tell.
